paragraphs: A learn-to-defer system decides both what prediction to make and when to hand a task to a human expert. Optimizing the accuracy of this partnership is only part of the problem: the system may also need to respect fairness requirements, limits on expert involvement, or rules about deferring unusual cases. This paper develops a common framework for handling several such requirements together.

The mathematical contribution extends the Neyman–Pearson lemma to multiple dimensions. Using this result, the authors derive a Bayes-optimal solution for constrained deferral decisions. They then design an algorithm that estimates this solution, connecting the theoretical decision rule to a procedure that can be applied to datasets.

On COMPAS, Hatespeech, and ACSIncome, the algorithm reduces constraint violations relative to the tested learn-to-defer baselines and controls several violations simultaneously. The contribution therefore concerns the balance between team performance and operational requirements. The authors also suggest that the mathematical framework could support other decision problems involving multiple controlled expected performance measures.
neurips-2024-a-unifying-post-processing-.tldr: A unified framework derives and estimates optimal human–AI deferral decisions under multiple constraints.

paragraphs: Language models can reproduce passages from their training data, creating privacy and copyright concerns. This paper addresses that behavior by changing the objective used during training. The proposed goldfish loss keeps the next-token prediction setting but leaves a randomly selected subset of tokens out of the loss calculation.

The central idea is to interrupt the learning signal that supports exact reproduction of a complete passage. According to the authors, the omitted tokens are not memorized, breaking the chain needed to repeat an entire training sequence verbatim. The intervention therefore operates at the level of which token predictions contribute to training, targeting memorization through a small change to the objective.

The authors test the method with billion-scale LLaMA-2 models, including models that were already pretrained and models trained from scratch. They report substantial reductions in extractable memorization with little or no effect on the downstream benchmarks evaluated. These findings support goldfish loss as a way to reduce recoverable training text while retaining measured task performance.
neurips-2024-be-like-a-goldfish-don-t-me.tldr: Goldfish loss omits randomly selected tokens from training loss to reduce extractable memorization with little measured downstream impact.

paragraphs: Bias can change during training as a model learns to rely on different features. Looking only at the beginning and end can miss these shifts, including periods when performance favors different parts of the population. This paper studies the intermediate dynamics of bias and asks which properties of the data influence them.

The authors use a teacher–student setup with a Gaussian-mixture model representing distinct subpopulations. Within this setting, they derive an analytical description of how a linear classifier evolves under stochastic gradient descent and prove that the description is exact in high dimension. Their analysis shows that different subpopulation properties drive bias on different timescales, causing the classifier's preferences to shift during training.

Applying the solution to fairness and robustness reveals how population differences and spurious features can produce or amplify bias over time. Experiments with deeper networks on synthetic data, CIFAR10, MNIST, and CelebA support the findings in more complex settings. The result makes training dynamics part of the explanation for unequal model behavior.
neurips-2024-bias-in-motion-theoretical-.tldr: An analysis of SGD shows how different population properties drive shifting model biases at different stages of training.

paragraphs: Event sequences can contain both immediate and delayed relationships: one event may trigger another straight away or after a changing interval. This paper introduces a causal model that represents those event-level triggering relationships with dynamic delays. The authors show that their model is identifiable for both instantaneous and delayed effects, addressing a difficulty for existing Granger-causality approaches.

Their method selects causal explanations through a description-length principle. The theoretical starting point is the Algorithmic Markov Condition, which favors the causal network with the smallest Kolmogorov complexity. Because that complexity cannot be computed, the authors build a practical score using Minimum Description Length and show that it identifies causal direction.

The proposed Cascade algorithm searches for a causal graph by adding edges in topological order. Evaluations report better performance than existing methods in settings containing instantaneous effects, noise, and multiple colliders, where several causes converge on an effect. Applications to real data also yield informative causal graphs. Together, the model and score connect local event attribution to discovery of broader causal structure.
neurips-2024-causal-discovery-from-event.tldr: Cascade discovers causal event networks using a description-length score that handles both immediate and delayed effects.

paragraphs: Linear bandit learners choose actions while learning from rewards, but corrupted feedback can distort those decisions. This paper brings two corruption settings into a unified analysis: strong corruption can depend on the chosen action, while weak corruption cannot. The distinction matters because the adversary's access changes the learning difficulty.

For stochastic linear bandits, the authors fully characterize the gap between the best achievable worst-case regret under these two settings. Regret measures the performance lost through learning decisions. They also study corrupted adversarial linear bandits, establishing upper and lower bounds whose dependence on the amount of corruption matches.

A further contribution links corruption resistance to gap-dependent misspecification, where model error scales with how suboptimal an action or policy is. A general reduction lets corruption-robust algorithms handle this setting and extends results to linear Markov decision processes. However, that reduction does not achieve the optimal rate. The authors therefore develop a specialized linear-bandit algorithm that attains optimal bounds for gap-dependent misspecification.
neurips-2024-corruption-robust-linear-ba.tldr: A unified theory distinguishes strong and weak reward corruption and connects robust bandit learning to model misspecification.

paragraphs: Cross-Care examines whether language models represent disease prevalence accurately across demographic groups. Its central concern is that patterns in training text may differ from actual population health patterns. If models carry those textual patterns into their outputs, their apparent medical knowledge can misrepresent how common diseases are among different groups.

The benchmark framework studies demographic biases in pretraining corpora such as ThePile and evaluates their influence on model outputs. It compares those representations with actual disease prevalence across demographic groups in the United States. This comparison gives the evaluation an external reference, allowing the authors to quantify discrepancies between model representations and population prevalence.

The results show substantial misalignment across demographic subgroups, indicating risks of bias propagation and weak grounding for medical applications. The authors also find that the alignment methods examined do little to resolve inconsistencies in disease-prevalence representations across languages. They release the data and a visualization tool to support further examination of these patterns.
neurips-2024-cross-care-assessing-the-he.tldr: Cross-Care finds substantial mismatches between language-model representations of disease prevalence and actual rates across demographic groups.

paragraphs: A classifier backdoor makes inputs containing a particular trigger receive an attacker-selected label. Existing approaches described in this paper require clean training data for retraining or changes to the model architecture. DFBA investigates whether a backdoor can be introduced without either requirement, reducing the resources and visible structural changes associated with the attack.

The method modifies a small number of classifier parameters while leaving the architecture intact and avoiding retraining. The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing that, under mild assumptions, the inserted backdoor cannot be detected or removed by various defenses considered in their analysis. That guarantee is conditional on those assumptions and concerns the specified defenses.

Across multiple evaluated datasets, the authors report negligible classification loss, a 100% attack success rate, and successful evasion of six existing defenses. A comparison with a non-data-free attack also finds better stealth and effectiveness against defenses, with less classification accuracy loss. The findings expose a vulnerability in which ordinary predictive performance can remain largely intact despite malicious trigger behavior.
neurips-2024-data-free-backdoor-attacks-.tldr: DFBA inserts classifier backdoors through a few parameter changes without training data, retraining, or architecture changes.

paragraphs: Diffusion Forcing connects causal sequence prediction with diffusion-based generation. Its defining training choice is to give individual tokens independent noise levels and teach a model to denoise them. This allows different positions in a sequence to have different degrees of uncertainty, rather than requiring a single noise level throughout.

Applied to a causal next-token model, the method can generate one or several future tokens without fully noising the past. The authors show that it combines variable-length generation with the ability to guide sampling toward desirable trajectories. Its causal structure and flexible generation horizon also support new ways of sampling and guiding sequences.

Experiments demonstrate continuous-token rollouts, including video, extending beyond the training horizon in settings where the tested baselines diverge. The authors also report marked gains in decision-making and planning tasks. Alongside these empirical findings, they prove that the method optimizes a variational lower bound on the likelihoods of all token subsequences drawn from the true joint distribution.
neurips-2024-diffusion-forcing-next-toke.tldr: Diffusion Forcing uses independent token noise levels to combine flexible causal generation with diffusion-based trajectory guidance.

paragraphs: Feature unlearning aims to remove a model's reliance on particular input features, including sensitive attributes, backdoor signals, or biased cues. In federated learning, this is complicated by methods that require other clients to participate in the removal process. The paper identifies that participation requirement as a practical obstacle for existing influence-function approaches.

Ferrari introduces feature sensitivity as a way to evaluate and pursue unlearning. Defined through Lipschitz continuity, the measure describes how quickly model outputs change when the targeted input feature is perturbed. The framework then minimizes this sensitivity, making reduced responsiveness to the feature the central optimization objective.

This connects the desired behavior after unlearning to a measurable property of the model: changes in the targeted feature should have less influence on its outputs. The authors support Ferrari with theoretical analysis and extensive experiments covering sensitive, backdoor, and biased features. Their findings indicate that sensitivity optimization can provide an effective framework for feature unlearning in federated settings.
neurips-2024-ferrari-federated-feature-u.tldr: Ferrari pursues federated feature unlearning by measuring and minimizing how strongly model outputs respond to targeted features.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can perform well on ordinary inputs while remaining vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. This paper investigates an aspect of that vulnerability that receives less attention than preprocessing or message-passing defenses: the weights used at initialization and how long the network is subsequently trained.

The authors develop a theoretical framework connecting initial weights, the number of training epochs, and susceptibility to adversarial changes. This makes robustness partly a question about the training process itself. Although graph neural networks are the main focus, the analysis also supplies a general upper bound applicable to deep neural networks.

Experiments across different models, real datasets, and adversarial attacks support the theoretical findings. The authors report that suitable initialization can preserve performance on clean data while improving robustness, with observed gaps reaching 50% relative to alternative initializations. That figure describes the reported experimental comparisons. The broader implication is that initialization and training duration deserve attention when evaluating or improving a model's resistance to adversarial inputs.
neurips-2024-if-you-want-to-be-robust-be.tldr: Theory and experiments connect neural-network initialization and training duration to adversarial robustness, with large observed differences between initializations.

paragraphs: Can repeated interaction let a strategic player overcome incomplete knowledge of a game? This paper studies that question using the player's Stackelberg value as the target outcome. Players choose learning algorithms that respond to observed histories and their existing knowledge, so learning behavior is itself part of strategic decision-making.

The authors analyze pure Nash equilibria of a meta-game whose actions are those algorithms. When one player knows the game perfectly, there is always such an equilibrium where that player obtains her Stackelberg value. However, they exhibit a game where no pure Nash equilibrium lets the partially informed player obtain her own Stackelberg value. Repeated interaction therefore does not guarantee that the informational disadvantage disappears.

When both players begin with uncertainty, information quality alone no longer determines who can attain the target value. The answer also depends on the game's structure. These results show why learning from another strategic learner can differ from simply collecting more observations: the other player's algorithm is also chosen to serve that player's interests.
neurips-2024-is-knowledge-power-on-the-i.tldr: Repeated strategic interaction need not let a partially informed player attain her Stackelberg value, and information advantages depend on game structure.

paragraphs: Estimating point-process models with maximum likelihood can require computationally difficult intensity integrals. Score matching is attractive because it avoids calculating those integrals. This paper asks whether existing score-matching estimators provide a sound replacement across general point processes, rather than only the specific problems where they have been used.

The authors show that some previously proposed estimators are incomplete, restricting their applicability and causing them to fail on more general point processes. They address this issue by introducing a weighted score-matching estimator. A theoretical consistency result supports the proposed estimator's statistical validity, giving the alternative an explicit foundation beyond its computational appeal.

Experiments examine both synthetic and real data. On synthetic data, the proposed method accurately estimates model parameters; on real data, it produces results consistent with maximum likelihood estimation. The existing score-matching estimators tested do not perform effectively. The contribution is therefore a repair to how score matching is applied to point processes, retaining the attraction of avoiding intensity integrals while addressing a demonstrated estimation failure.
neurips-2024-is-score-matching-suitable-.tldr: A consistent weighted score-matching estimator addresses failures of earlier point-process estimators while avoiding intensity integrals.

paragraphs: Causal bandit algorithms learn which interventions produce desirable outcomes. Many approaches assume either a known causal graph or restrictive interventions that remove randomness and dependencies on upstream variables. This paper tackles linear causal bandits when both the graph and the stochastic intervention models are unknown.

The authors provide a computationally efficient algorithm together with upper and minimax lower regret bounds. Regret captures the accumulated cost of learning which interventions to choose. Both bounds scale with the square root of the number of interaction rounds. They also expose exponential dependence on the longest causal path and polynomial dependence on maximum in-degree, with a remaining gap in the bounds.

The upper bound includes the number of graph nodes through an additive term involving intervention power. Consequently, graph size has a diminishing relative influence as interaction rounds accumulate. The results clarify how causal depth, connectivity, and intervention power shape learning difficulty while addressing the computational challenge associated with algorithms that use soft, stochastic interventions.
neurips-2024-linear-causal-bandits-unkno.tldr: An efficient linear causal-bandit algorithm handles unknown graphs and stochastic interventions, with regret bounds exposing the role of causal structure.

paragraphs: Understanding brain-wide communication requires considering relationships that extend beyond nearby regions in a brain network. The paper argues that an emphasis on short-range dependencies limits that understanding. It introduces ALTER, a brain graph transformer designed to incorporate long-range relationships alongside shorter-range connections.

ALTER uses biased random walks to capture extended dependencies between brain regions of interest. At each step, the walk favors a next region with a higher correlation value. This supplies the model with paths intended to represent broader brain communication. A transformer then adaptively integrates information from both short- and long-range dependencies, combining multiple levels of network relationships.

The authors evaluate ALTER on ABIDE and ADNI for neurological disease diagnosis. They report consistent improvements over the tested general-purpose graph-learning methods and methods developed specifically for brain-network analysis. These findings support the usefulness of explicitly modeling longer-range connectivity for the evaluated diagnostic tasks. The contribution ties a particular graph exploration strategy to a model that can combine local and extended information.
neurips-2024-long-range-brain-graph-tran.tldr: ALTER combines correlation-guided random walks and a transformer to model long-range brain connectivity and improve evaluated diagnostic performance.

paragraphs: Choosing brain-stimulation settings becomes difficult when many electrode combinations and other parameters are available. A predictive model could guide the search, but one experimental session may provide too few examples. Combining sessions introduces another challenge because recorded neural activity changes over time.

MiSO addresses both problems through a closed-loop framework. It first aligns neural activity across sessions so their stimulation-response samples can be combined. A statistical model learns from those samples to predict responses to untested configurations. An online optimizer then uses those predictions to adaptively choose stimulation settings. The implementation uses factor analysis for alignment, a convolutional neural network for prediction, and epsilon-greedy optimization.

The authors test MiSO with electrical microstimulation in the prefrontal cortex of a non-human primate. Guided by model predictions, it successfully searches thousands of parameter configurations and moves neural population activity toward specified states. This demonstrates how combining data across sessions with adaptive search can make larger stimulation spaces usable, supporting the framework's proposed relevance to neuromodulation.
neurips-2024-miso-optimizing-brain-stimu.tldr: MiSO combines cross-session neural alignment, response prediction, and adaptive search to steer neural activity through brain stimulation.

paragraphs: Segmenting kidneys and tumors across multiple MRI sequences can require detailed annotations for each sequence. Unsupervised domain adaptation reduces that burden by transferring across imaging domains. However, handling each target through a separate one-to-one transfer can be inefficient. PSTUDA introduces a one-to-multiple framework to address several target domains together.

The method stores target-domain style information in a dictionary at multiple levels. This helps separate image content from domain-specific appearance and reduces the burden placed on a single generator. Cascading style-fusion modules then progressively recombine content and style using point-wise instance normalization, supporting alignment across modalities while maintaining structural consistency.

Experiments on the private MSKT and public KiTS19 datasets show improvements over the compared segmentation methods, with reported average Dice Similarity Coefficient gains of at least 1.8% and 3.9%, respectively. The framework also reduces floating-point computation by approximately 72% and parameter count by about 50%. Together, these findings support a more efficient approach to adapting kidney and tumor segmentation across multiple imaging targets.
neurips-2024-one-to-multiple-a-progressi.tldr: PSTUDA progressively transfers image styles across multiple MRI targets, improving evaluated segmentation while reducing computation and model size.

paragraphs: This paper develops a PAC-Bayes oracle bound for losses that are not restricted to a fixed upper limit. It extends Cramér–Chernoff bounds into the PAC-Bayesian setting, connecting a way of controlling tail behavior with bounds that apply to distributions over models. The aim is to obtain informative guarantees under richer assumptions about the loss.

The proof controls tails of random variables involving the loss's Cramér transform. This construction carries useful features of Cramér–Chernoff analysis into the resulting bounds, including exact optimization of a free parameter appearing in many PAC-Bayes formulations. The authors show that their theorem recovers earlier results and extends them.

They also introduce a model-dependent assumption that yields bounds involving parameter norms and log-Sobolev inequalities. These richer assumptions can make the guarantees more informative and potentially tighter. Minimizing many of the resulting bounds produces distributions beyond the Gibbs posterior. This gives theoretical coverage to existing regularization techniques while broadening the kinds of model distributions supported by the analysis.
neurips-2024-pac-bayes-chernoff-bounds-f.tldr: New PAC-Bayes bounds extend Cramér–Chernoff analysis to unbounded losses and support richer assumptions and model distributions.

paragraphs: A language model may perform well on a benchmark partly because related test material appeared in its training data. RepLiQA addresses this evaluation problem with reference documents describing imaginary scenarios written by human annotators. Answering questions about these scenarios requires using the supplied document's content.

Each sample includes a reference document, a question, an answer derived from that document, and the paragraph containing the answer. These components connect the expected response to explicit evidence in the reference. The dataset contains five test splits, four of which had not been released online or exposed to language-model APIs before the paper's publication.

The authors use RepLiQA to benchmark several leading language models of different types and sizes in a setting where answers depend on provided context. The evaluation uncovers differences in model performance, and the dataset also supports topic retrieval. Its contribution is a controlled way to test whether models can locate and use unfamiliar reference information, reducing the ambiguity introduced by possible overlap between training material and benchmark content.
neurips-2024-repliqa-a-question-answerin.tldr: RepLiQA tests language models on human-written imaginary documents to assess their use of unfamiliar reference content.

paragraphs: Contextual sparsity reduces language-model inference costs without additional training, but its effects depend on the task. The authors find that methods performing well on prompt understanding can substantially degrade reasoning, deduction, and knowledge-based generation. This motivates examining where sparse generation goes wrong.

Their key observation is that sparse and original models often follow similar overall problem-solving logic. In those cases, correcting only a few tokens can recover the original model's performance. SIRIUS introduces an efficient correction mechanism built around this observation, improving reasoning performance while preserving efficiency gains from sparsity.

Evaluation spans six models and eight challenging generation tasks involving reasoning, deduction, and coding. The authors report consistent effectiveness and efficiency across these tests. They also develop a system implementation and report roughly 20% lower latency for an on-chip 8B model and 35% lower latency for a 70B model using offloading. These results show how targeted corrections can help turn sparsity's computational savings into usable generation speedups on demanding tasks.
neurips-2024-sirius-contexual-sparisty-w.tldr: SIRIUS corrects sparse language-model generation to improve difficult-task performance while retaining inference speedups.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time series together requires modeling both how each series evolves and how the series relate to one another. Those relationships can have structure and change over time. The paper identifies a problem with approaches that first learn dynamic representations and then generate relationships: short input windows can make the resulting structures unstable.

The proposed model generates dynamic spatial structures using a structured matrix basis. Its parameterization and structural regularization constrain the space of relationships the model can produce. The authors describe the resulting structures as having lower variance while retaining greater expressiveness and offering interpretable dynamics.

This design places structure directly into the mechanism that generates relationships, addressing the instability of the two-stage approach. Across six benchmark datasets, the forecasting model achieves improvements of up to 8.5% over existing methods. It also provides insights into the dynamics of the underlying systems. The contribution therefore combines predictive gains with a representation of changing cross-series relationships that can help explain the model's view of the system.
neurips-2024-structured-matrix-basis-for.tldr: A structured matrix basis models changing relationships among time series, improving forecasting and making dynamics more interpretable.

paragraphs: Supervised learning for integer linear programs can pair each problem with an optimal solution. Symmetry complicates this setup: permuting variables may preserve the problem while producing multiple equivalent optimal solutions. Selecting one arbitrarily as the label creates variation that can make stable patterns harder for a model to learn.

SymILO incorporates these equivalences into training. It treats the permutation of a solution as something to learn alongside the neural-network weights. An alternating algorithm jointly optimizes the loss by updating these learnable components. This lets the training process account for the fact that different-looking labels may represent equivalent answers to the same optimization structure.

The authors evaluate the framework on integer linear programs with different symmetries. They report average improvements of 50.3%, 66.5%, and 45.4% over three existing methods, respectively. The findings support making solution symmetry part of the supervised learning task itself. The broader contribution is a way to reduce the learning difficulty created by arbitrary choices among equally valid optimal labels.
neurips-2024-symilo-a-symmetry-aware-lea.tldr: SymILO learns solution permutations alongside network weights to account for equivalent optimal labels in symmetric integer linear programs.

paragraphs: An optimizer can influence which classifier emerges from training, beyond its role in reducing the training objective. This preference is called implicit bias. The paper studies that preference for Adam in linear logistic regression, focusing on data that are linearly separable: a linear boundary can separate the training classes.

The authors prove that Adam's iterates approach the direction of a classifier achieving the maximum margin defined using the infinity norm. The result concerns the direction of the classifier's weights, which determines the separating boundary. It identifies a specific geometric preference in Adam's training dynamics within this setting.

For a general class of diminishing learning rates, the authors also establish polynomial-time convergence to that direction. This adds a statement about the rate of the process to the description of its eventual preference. Together, the results provide a theoretical basis for distinguishing Adam from gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent. The claims apply to the stated linear, separable-data setting, where the optimizer's implicit choice can be characterized precisely.
neurips-2024-the-implicit-bias-of-adam-o.tldr: On linearly separable logistic-regression data, Adam converges in direction toward a maximum infinity-norm-margin classifier.

paragraphs: Circuit analysis seeks small collections of model components that explain particular behaviors. Transformer MLP layers make this difficult because an interpretable feature can combine many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity. Following all those contributions can create unwieldy circuits or blur the distinction between local behavior and broader model structure.

The paper explores transcoders, which approximate a densely active MLP with a wider MLP that activates sparsely. The authors introduce a method for tracing circuits through these approximations using their weights. The resulting circuits separate into terms that depend on the input and terms that remain fixed across inputs, making the computation easier to examine.

Transcoders trained on models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters perform at least as well as sparse autoencoders on the evaluated sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability criteria. The authors also use them to investigate previously unknown circuits and gain new insights into GPT2-small's greater-than circuit. These findings suggest that transcoders can make computations involving MLPs more accessible to circuit-level interpretation.
neurips-2024-transcoders-find-interpreta.tldr: Transcoders approximate dense MLPs with sparse alternatives that support interpretable, weights-based analysis of language-model circuits.

paragraphs: Some tasks begin without enough information to solve them. A useful assistant must decide what to ask next, as in diagnosis or troubleshooting. Uncertainty of Thoughts addresses this information-seeking problem by giving language models a planning procedure for choosing effective follow-up questions.

The algorithm combines three mechanisms. It simulates possible future scenarios while accounting for how likely they are. Rewards based on uncertainty and motivated by information gain encourage questions that reveal useful information. A reward-propagation scheme then selects the question with the highest expected reward. Together, these components connect the model's uncertainty to its choice of what to ask.

The authors evaluate the method on medical diagnosis, troubleshooting, and the 20 Questions game across multiple language models. Compared with direct prompting, it delivers a reported average improvement of 38.1% in successful task completion and also improves efficiency measured by the number of questions required. The findings support explicitly planning information gathering when answering well depends on acquiring details that were initially missing.
neurips-2024-uncertainty-of-thoughts-unc.tldr: Uncertainty of Thoughts plans follow-up questions using simulated outcomes and information-based rewards, improving task success and question efficiency.

paragraphs: Web content often mixes images and text in a sequence rather than presenting isolated image–caption pairs. Latent Compression Learning introduces a vision pretraining method designed to use this interleaved material. It connects visual representations to both the text that comes before an image and the text that follows it.

The training objective maximizes mutual information between a causal attention model's inputs and outputs. The authors decompose this objective into two tasks: contrastive learning between a visual representation and its preceding context, and generation of subsequent text from that representation. These tasks provide complementary training signals from the surrounding sequence.

Experiments show that the method matches CLIP's performance on paired pretraining data such as LAION. It also learns robust visual representations from scratch using interleaved data such as MMC4. The findings demonstrate that the same approach can work with paired examples while taking advantage of the richer arrangement of images and text found in interleaved material, expanding the forms of web data available for vision pretraining.
neurips-2024-vision-model-pre-training-o.tldr: Latent Compression Learning trains visual representations from interleaved images and text using preceding-context contrast and subsequent-text generation.
